propositions.text: The Criminal Code allows time served in remand to be credited towards a sentence of imprisonment.
propositions.quote: When an accused person is not granted bail, and must be remanded in jail awaiting trial, the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , allows time served to be credited towards a resulting sentence of imprisonment.

propositions.text: A day in jail should count as a day in jail for credit purposes.
propositions.quote: A day in jail should count as a day in jail.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Criminal Code allows credit for time served in remand and that a day in jail counts as a day in jail.

propositions.text: Crediting one day per day in remand is often insufficient to reflect the full impact of detention.
propositions.quote: However, crediting a single day for every day spent in a remand centre is often insufficient to account for the full impact of that detention, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

propositions.text: Time in remand does not count towards parole eligibility, earned remission, or statutory release, leading to longer incarceration.
propositions.quote: Time in a remand centre does not count for the purposes of eligibility for parole, earned remission or statutory release, and this can result in a longer term of actual incarceration for offenders who were denied bail.

propositions.text: Remand centre conditions tend to be harsh, overcrowded, dangerous, and lack rehabilitative programs.
propositions.quote: Moreover, conditions in remand centres tend to be particularly harsh; they are often overcrowded and dangerous, and do not provide rehabilitative programs.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that one-for-one credit often fails to reflect harsher conditions and parole ineligibility in remand centres.

propositions.text: Courts frequently granted enhanced credit of 2 days per day in pre-sentence custody for many years.
propositions.quote: As a result, for many years courts frequently granted “enhanced” credit: 2 days for each day spent in pre-sentence custody.

propositions.text: This practice was endorsed by the Supreme Court in R. v. Wust, 2000 SCC 18.
propositions.quote: This practice was endorsed by this Court in R. v. Wust, 2000 SCC 18, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 455.

propositions.text: Judges granted credit at 3 to 1 or more when conditions were exceptionally harsh.
propositions.quote: When conditions were exceptionally harsh, judges granted credit at a rate of 3 to 1 or more.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes courts granted enhanced credit, endorsed by R. v. Wust, sometimes up to 3 to 1 for harsh conditions.

propositions.text: The Truth in Sentencing Act (TISA) amended the Criminal Code to cap pre-sentence credit at 1.5 days per day in custody.
propositions.quote: The Truth in Sentencing Act, S.C. 2009, c. 29 (TISA ), passed in 2009, amended the Criminal Code to cap pre-sentence credit at a maximum of 1.5 days for every day in custody.

propositions.text: The purpose was to remove incentives to prolong remand and provide transparency about sentencing credit.
propositions.quote: The purpose was to remove any incentive for an accused to drag out time in remand custody, and to provide transparency so that the public would know what the fit sentence was, how much credit had been given, and why.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains TISA capped pre-sentence credit at 1.5 to 1 to prevent delays and increase transparency.

propositions.text: The Court must interpret the amendments regarding when enhanced credit above 1 to 1 is available.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Court is called upon to interpret these amendments. There is no dispute that Parliament imposed a cap on enhanced credit at a rate of 1.5 to 1. However, there are conflicting lower court decisions on when “enhanced” credit at a rate higher than 1 to 1 is available.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue of interpreting when enhanced credit above one-to-one is available under the amendments.

propositions.text: The statute states enhanced credit is available when 'the circumstances justify it' but is otherwise silent.
propositions.quote: The statute does not definitively address the issue, providing simply that enhanced credit is available when “the circumstances justify it” (s. 719(3.1) ).

propositions.text: The legislative history is contradictory and inconclusive.
propositions.quote: The legislative history is contradictory and inconclusive.

propositions.text: The Court must determine what 'circumstances' justify enhanced credit up to 1.5 to 1.
propositions.quote: We must interpret the provisions to determine what “circumstances” justify enhanced credit of up to a rate of 1.5 to 1.

propositions.text: The Attorney General of Ontario argues loss of parole eligibility cannot justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1).
propositions.quote: The appellant, the Attorney General of Ontario, argues that the loss of eligibility for parole and statutory release cannot be a “circumstance” justifying enhanced credit under the new s. 719(3.1) of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: Ontario and Nova Scotia Courts of Appeal held loss of parole eligibility is a 'circumstance' justifying enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: The Ontario Court of Appeal in this case and the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in the companion case, R. v. Carvery, 2012 NSCA 107, 321 N.S.R. (2d) 321, came to the opposite conclusion, and held that the loss of eligibility for parole and statutory release is a “circumstance” that can justify enhanced credit.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the statute's silence, conflicting appellate decisions, and the Attorney General's argument against parole loss as a justifying circumstance.

propositions.text: TISA caps pre-sentence credit but does not limit the 'circumstances' justifying enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: In my view, while the Truth in Sentencing Act caps pre-sentence credit, it does not limit the “circumstances” that justify granting credit.

propositions.text: Parliament expressly altered maximum credit but excluded no particular 'circumstances' from consideration.
propositions.quote: Where Parliament intended to alter existing practice, as with respect to the maximum amount of credit, it did so expressly. However, the legislation excludes no particular “circumstances” from consideration.

propositions.text: If Parliament intended to exclude loss of early release eligibility as a circumstance, it would have done so expressly.
propositions.quote: Had Parliament intended to alter the well-established rule that enhanced credit compensates for the loss of eligibility for early release, it would have done so expressly.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes TISA caps credit but does not exclude any circumstances, including loss of early release eligibility, from justifying enhanced credit.

propositions.text: The appeal concerns amendments to s. 719(3) and (3.1) of the Criminal Code from TISA.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns amendments to s. 719(3) of the Criminal Code , resulting from the TISA .

propositions.text: Sections 719(3) and (3.1) now limit credit to one day per day, or 1.5 days if circumstances justify it, with exceptions.
propositions.quote: Sections 719(3) and 719(3.1) now read (changes underlined): (3) In determining the sentence to be imposed on a person convicted of an offence, a court may take into account any time spent in custody by the person as a result of the offence but the court shall limit any credit for that time to a maximum of one day for each day spent in custody. (3.1) Despite subsection (3), if the circumstances justify it, the maximum is one and one-half days for each day spent in custody unless the reason for detaining the person in custody was stated in the record under subsection 515(9.1) or the person was detained in custody under subsection 524(4) or (8) .

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appeal concerns TISA amendments limiting credit to one day per day or 1.5 days if circumstances justify it, with exceptions.

propositions.text: Sean Summers violently shook his infant daughter, causing her death; charged with manslaughter after initial murder charge.
propositions.quote: On July 9, 2010, Sean Summers, the respondent, violently shook his infant daughter, resulting in her death three days later. He was initially arrested on a charge of second degree murder but, in April 2011, that information was withdrawn and he was charged with manslaughter.

propositions.text: He pleaded guilty to manslaughter on May 30, 2011.
propositions.quote: On May 30, 2011, he pleaded guilty to manslaughter.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts Summers' offense, charge change, and guilty plea to manslaughter.

propositions.text: Summers was in custody for 10.5 months from arrest until guilty plea and sentencing.
propositions.quote: The respondent was in custody for a period of 10.5 months, from his arrest in July 2010 until he pleaded guilty and was sentenced, in May 2011.

propositions.text: No suggestion that detention conditions were unusually harsh.
propositions.quote: There has been no suggestion that the conditions of detention were unusually harsh.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Summers' 10.5 months custody and no claim of harsh detention conditions.

propositions.text: Counsel agreed sentence range was 8 to 10 years imprisonment.
propositions.quote: Counsel agreed that an appropriate range for the sentence was between eight and ten years’ imprisonment.

paragraphs.summary: The sentencing counsel agreed on an 8 to 10 year imprisonment range.

propositions.text: Defence argued for 1.5 days credit per day due to lost eligibility for early release and parole.
propositions.quote: Defence counsel argued that the respondent should receive credit at a rate of 1.5 days for every day in custody; the lost eligibility for early release and parole while in remand custody was a circumstance justifying the application of s. 719(3.1) of the Code.

propositions.text: Crown did not object to 1.5 to 1 credit for first six months while awaiting post-mortem report.
propositions.quote: The Crown did not object to granting credit for the first six months of detention at a rate of 1.5 to 1; during this time, the accused was waiting for a post-mortem report to be disclosed.

propositions.text: Crown invited judge to use discretion for credit for remaining detention period.
propositions.quote: As for the rest of the detention, the Crown invited the judge to use his discretion in assessing credit.

paragraphs.summary: Defence sought 1.5 to 1 credit for lost parole eligibility; Crown agreed for six months and left rest to judge's discretion.

propositions.text: Judge reasoned enhanced credit based on lost parole eligibility is equitable and justified under s. 719(3.1).
propositions.quote: The sentencing judge, Glithero J., of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, reasoned that the traditional practice of granting credit at a rate of two days for every day in detention was based upon the fact that time served on remand did not count towards parole eligibility. Since most offenders are released on parole between the one-third and two-third marks of their sentences, it would be inequitable not to give enhanced credit to reflect time in pre-trial custody. The fact that pre-trial detention did not count towards parole eligibility for the respondent was a circumstance justifying credit at a ratio of 1.5:1 under s. 719(3.1) of the Code.

paragraphs.summary: The sentencing judge found lost parole eligibility justified enhanced credit at 1.5 to 1 under s. 719(3.1).

propositions.text: Respondent sentenced to 8 years minus 16 months credit for 10.5 months pre-trial custody, resulting in 6 years 8 months.
propositions.quote: The judge sentenced the respondent to 8 years’ imprisonment, less a credit of 16 months for 10.5 months of pre-trial detention. This resulted in a sentence of 6 years and 8 months.

paragraphs.summary: The judge sentenced Summers to 6 years 8 months after enhanced credit for pre-trial custody.

propositions.text: Crown appealed arguing s. 719(3.1) does not allow 1.5:1 credit solely for lost early release and parole eligibility.
propositions.quote: The Crown appealed on the basis that, under s. 719(3.1) , credit cannot be assigned at a rate of 1.5:1 solely to account for an accused’s loss of eligibility for early release and parole.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown appealed, arguing enhanced credit cannot be granted solely for lost early release eligibility.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) is not limited to exceptional circumstances and can be justified by lost parole eligibility.
propositions.quote: Cronk J.A., writing for the Court of Appeal, concluded that enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) was not limited to exceptional circumstances and could be justified on the basis of lost eligibility for early release and parole.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal interpreted s. 719(3.1) considering TISA text, history, and sentencing principles.
propositions.quote: She engaged in a thoughtful and thorough interpretation of s. 719(3.1) , considering the text of the TISA , its legislative history, and the principles that underpin the Criminal Code sentencing scheme.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found lost parole eligibility can justify enhanced credit and thoroughly interpreted s. 719(3.1).

propositions.text: Not every remand offender gets enhanced credit for lost parole eligibility; it depends on likelihood of early release and judge's discretion.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal clarified that not every remand offender will be granted enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) on the basis of lost eligibility for early release and parole. These may be circumstances justifying credit, but only if the accused would probably have received early release or parole. A judge retains the discretion to deny credit at the enhanced rate, for example when an accused intentionally delayed proceedings.

propositions.text: Certain offenders are excluded from s. 719(3.1) and get no more than one-for-one credit under s. 719(3).
propositions.quote: Certain offenders are expressly excluded from s. 719(3.1) , and are therefore entitled to no more than one-for-one pre-trial credit under s. 719(3) .

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal held enhanced credit depends on probable early release and discretion; some offenders are excluded.

propositions.text: No error in granting Summers enhanced credit at 1.5:1 given no basis to deny lost parole eligibility credit.
propositions.quote: Given that there was no basis to conclude that the respondent would have been denied parole or early release, there was no error in granting enhanced credit at a rate of 1.5:1 to account for lost early release and parole eligibility.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found no error in granting Summers enhanced credit for lost parole eligibility.

propositions.text: Is loss of early release and parole eligibility a 'circumstance' justifying enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1)?
propositions.quote: Is ineligibility for early release and parole while on remand a “circumstance” that can justify granting enhanced credit for pre-sentence custody under s. 719(3.1) of the Criminal Code ?

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue whether loss of early release eligibility justifies enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1).

propositions.text: Before TISA, s. 719(3) allowed courts to credit any time spent in custody without restrictions.
propositions.quote: Prior to the enactment of the TISA in 2009, s. 719(3) of the Criminal Code simply provided that a sentencing court “may take into account any time spent in custody by the person as a result of the offence”.

propositions.text: R. v. Rezaie explained judges should not deny credit without good reason as incarceration denies liberty.
propositions.quote: In R. v. Rezaie (1996), 31 O.R. (3d) 713, Laskin J.A. of the Ontario Court of Appeal explained the rationale for granting credit. He noted that a judge should not deny credit without good reason. To do so offends one’s sense of fairness. Incarceration at any stage of the criminal process is a denial of an accused’s liberty. [p. 721]

paragraphs.summary: The court recalls pre-TISA law allowed credit for all custody time and R. v. Rezaie emphasized fairness in granting credit.

propositions.text: It would be unfair if pre-sentence custody days were not credited towards the offender's ultimate sentence.
propositions.quote: it would be unfair if a day spent in custody, prior to sentencing, were not counted towards an offender’s ultimate sentence

propositions.text: A day of incarceration requires at least a credit of one day towards the sentence.
propositions.quote: a day of incarceration requires at least a credit of one day towards the sentence

paragraphs.summary: The court states that pre-sentence custody must be credited at least one day per day to avoid unfairness.

propositions.text: Courts gave enhanced credit recognizing pre-trial custody is more onerous than post-sentencing custody in two respects.
propositions.quote: Courts generally gave enhanced credit in recognition of the fact that “in two respects, pre-trial custody is even more onerous than post-sentencing custody” (Rezaie, at p. 721).

propositions.text: First, parole eligibility and statutory release do not consider pre-trial custody time.
propositions.quote: First, other than for a sentence of life imprisonment, legislative provisions for parole eligibility and statutory release do not take into account time spent in custody before trial (or before sentencing).

propositions.text: Second, local detention centres usually lack educational, retraining or rehabilitation programs for pre-trial detainees.
propositions.quote: Second, local detention centres ordinarily do not provide educational, retraining or rehabilitation programs to an accused in custody awaiting trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court states courts gave enhanced credit because pre-trial custody is more onerous due to parole rules and lack of programs.

propositions.text: The quantitative rationale for enhanced credit is to prevent offenders spending more time incarcerated than if released on bail.
propositions.quote: First, the quantitative rationale for the practice of granting enhanced credit is to ensure that the offender does not spend more time behind bars than if he had been released on bail.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the quantitative rationale for enhanced credit is to avoid longer incarceration than bail release.

propositions.text: Parole is available federally after one third of sentence served; statutory release after two thirds.
propositions.quote: Under the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, S.C. 1992, c. 20 (CCRA ), parole becomes available to a federal inmate after one third of the sentence has been served (s. 120 ), and statutory release is available once two thirds of the sentence has been served (s. 127(3) ).

propositions.text: Provincial inmates earn remission at 15 days per month, equivalent to federal statutory release.
propositions.quote: Provincial inmates can earn essentially equivalent “earned remission”, absent bad conduct, credited at 15 days per month as calculated under the federal Prisons and Reformatories Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-20, s. 6 .

propositions.text: Statutory release and earned remission are collectively called “early release” in these reasons.
propositions.quote: Throughout these reasons, I refer to statutory release and earned remission collectively as “early release”.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes parole and statutory release rules and defines “early release” as statutory release and remission.

propositions.text: Most reformatory sentence prisoners are released on remission at about two-thirds of sentence.
propositions.quote: In practice, the “vast majority of those serving reformatory sentences are released on ‘remission’ . . . at approximately the two-thirds point in their sentence”

propositions.text: Only 2-3% of federal prisoners are not released by parole or statutory release.
propositions.quote: only two to three percent of federal prisoners are not released either by way of parole or “statutory release”

paragraphs.summary: The court states most prisoners are released at two-thirds sentence by remission; few are not released early.

propositions.text: Sentences begin when imposed and parole rules exclude pre-sentence custody time.
propositions.quote: Because a sentence begins when it is imposed (s. 719(1)) and the statutory rules for parole eligibility and early release do not take into account time spent in custody before sentencing

propositions.text: Pre-sentence detention usually needs credit higher than 1:1 to avoid prejudice to offender.
propositions.quote: pre-sentence detention almost always needs to be credited at a rate higher than 1:1 in order to ensure that it does not prejudice the offender.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds pre-sentence detention needs enhanced credit because parole rules exclude that time.

propositions.text: A 1.5:1 credit ratio ensures equal jail time whether or not pre-sentence detention occurred.
propositions.quote: A ratio of 1.5:1 ensures that an offender who is released after serving two thirds of his sentence serves the same amount of time in jail, whether or not he is subject to pre-sentence detention.

propositions.text: Higher ratios than 1.5:1 were used to account for loss of parole eligibility and other circumstances.
propositions.quote: A higher ratio than 1.5:1 was therefore often used to account for other circumstances, including the loss of parole eligibility

paragraphs.summary: The court explains 1.5:1 credit matches jail time; higher ratios address parole loss and other factors.

propositions.text: Second rationale for enhanced credit is qualitative: pre-trial detention lacks programs and is more onerous.
propositions.quote: The second rationale for enhanced credit is qualitative in nature. Remand detention centres tend not to provide the educational, retraining or rehabilitation programs that are generally available when serving a sentence in corrections facilities.

propositions.text: Overcrowding, turnover, labour disputes make pre-sentence detention more onerous.
propositions.quote: overcrowding, inmate turnover, labour disputes and other factors also tend to make pre-sentence detention more onerous.

paragraphs.summary: The court states qualitative reasons for enhanced credit include lack of programs and harsh conditions in pre-trial detention.

propositions.text: Impact of overcrowding and lack of programs varies by offender's needs and disposition.
propositions.quote: The impact of overcrowding, or a lack of educational programs, varies depending on the particular offender’s needs, character and disposition.

propositions.text: Assigning enhanced credit on this basis is qualitative, fact-dependent and discretionary.
propositions.quote: Assigning enhanced credit on this basis is a qualitative, fact-dependent and discretionary exercise.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds enhanced credit assignment is fact-dependent and discretionary based on offender's needs and conditions.

propositions.text: Practice developed granting 2:1 credit for pre-sentence detention based on twin rationales.
propositions.quote: a practice developed over time of granting credit for pre-sentence detention at a rate of 2:1.

propositions.text: Wust endorsed 2:1 credit practice but said correct rate is not rigid and left to sentencing judge.
propositions.quote: In Wust, this Court endorsed this practice, but noted that the correct rate cannot be determined by a rigid formula, and is best left to the sentencing judge.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes 2:1 credit practice developed and Wust endorsed it but left rate to sentencing judge discretion.

propositions.text: When remand has full programs, less than 2:1 credit may be appropriate but some enhanced credit still given.
propositions.quote: when an accused was detained in a remand institution with full access to educational and rehabilitation programs, credit at a ratio of less than 2:1 was sometimes appropriate

propositions.text: Bad conduct causing extended pre-sentence detention militates against enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: when extended pre-sentence detention could be attributed to bad conduct on the part of the accused (such as breaching bail conditions), that militated against enhanced credit (Rezaie).

propositions.text: Harsh conditions may justify credit as high as 3:1 or 4:1 rarely.
propositions.quote: when an offender was subjected to particularly harsh conditions, rates as high as 3:1 or (rarely) 4:1 were sometimes applied.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains credit varies by conditions, bad conduct reduces credit, harsh conditions increase it.

propositions.text: In 2009, Parliament amended s. 719 to limit pre-trial custody credit to max 1:1, with possible 1.5:1 if circumstances justify.
propositions.quote: In 2009, Parliament changed the statutory regime governing credit for pre-sentence detention... limit credit for pre-trial custody “to a maximum of one day for each day spent in custody”. Second, Parliament provided in s. 719(3.1) that despite that limit, “if the circumstances justify it, the maximum is one and one-half days for each day spent in custody”

paragraphs.summary: The court states Parliament amended s. 719 to limit credit to 1:1, with 1.5:1 possible if circumstances justify.

propositions.text: The issue is the meaning of “circumstances” in s. 719(3.1) and if lost early release eligibility qualifies.
propositions.quote: Specifically, we must determine the meaning of “circumstances” in s. 719(3.1) , and whether the lost opportunity for early release and parole in pre-sentence detention can be such a circumstance

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue as interpreting “circumstances” in s. 719(3.1) and if lost early release counts.

propositions.text: Loss of parole and early release is a “circumstance” justifying enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: I conclude that loss of access to parole and early release constitutes a “circumstance” capable of justifying enhanced credit.

propositions.text: The court agrees with reasons of Cronk J.A. and Beveridge J.A. on this point.
propositions.quote: I am in substantial agreement with the exemplary reasons of both Cronk J.A. in this case, and Beveridge J.A. in the companion case Carvery.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes loss of parole eligibility is a circumstance justifying enhanced credit, agreeing with lower courts.

propositions.text: The court will analyze text, structure, intention, and scheme of Criminal Code for interpretation.
propositions.quote: In the reasons that follow, I discuss: (1) the text of the provision, (2) the structure of the section, (3) the intention of Parliament, and (4) the scheme of the Criminal Code

propositions.text: Meaning is clear by conventional statutory interpretation; no need to invoke Charter conformity presumption.
propositions.quote: the meaning of the provision is clear on the basis of conventional principles of statutory interpretation, and it is therefore neither appropriate nor necessary to have recourse to the presumption that the legislation conforms to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

paragraphs.summary: The court will interpret the provision by text, structure, intention, and scheme, without needing Charter presumption.

propositions.text: Section 719(3.1) states max credit is 1.5 days per day if circumstances justify, except for certain detention reasons.
propositions.quote: Section 719(3.1) reads as follows: (3.1) Despite subsection (3), if the circumstances justify it, the maximum is one and one-half days for each day spent in custody unless the reason for detaining the person in custody was stated in the record under subsection 515(9.1) or the person was detained in custody under subsection 524(4) or (8) .

paragraphs.summary: The court quotes s. 719(3.1) limiting enhanced credit to 1.5:1 if circumstances justify, except for specified detention reasons.

propositions.text: Provision does not limit what may constitute “circumstances”.
propositions.quote: this provision is free of any language limiting the scope of what may constitute “circumstances”.

propositions.text: Legislature could have limited “circumstances” to exclude loss of early release eligibility but did not.
propositions.quote: The legislature could easily have provided that only “exceptional circumstances” or “circumstances other than the loss of eligibility for early release and parole” justify enhanced credit.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s. 719(3.1) does not limit “circumstances” and legislature could have but did not exclude loss of early release.

propositions.text: Other Criminal Code provisions use limiting language like “exceptional” or “compelling circumstances”.
propositions.quote: language limiting the scope of the word “circumstances” is used elsewhere in the Criminal Code . For example, reference is made to “exceptional circumstances” or “compelling circumstances”

propositions.text: Examples include ss. 672.14(3), 672.47(2), and 742.6(16) using limiting language.

paragraphs.summary: The court observes other Criminal Code sections use limiting terms like “exceptional circumstances”.

propositions.text: Parliament restricted enhanced credit for offenders denied bail due to prior conviction or bail breaches.
propositions.quote: Parliament did restrict enhanced credit, withholding it from offenders who have been denied bail primarily as a result of a previous conviction (s. 515(9.1) ), those who contravened their bail conditions (ss. 524(4) (a) and 524(8) (a)), and those who committed an indictable offence while on bail (ss. 524(4) (b) and 524(8) (b)).

propositions.text: Parliament did not limit scope of “circumstances” justifying enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: Parliament clearly turned its attention to the circumstances under which s. 719(3.1) should not apply, but did not include any limitations on the scope of “circumstances” justifying its application.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Parliament limited enhanced credit for certain bail-related reasons but did not limit “circumstances” scope.

propositions.text: Crown concedes “circumstances” need not be exceptional but excludes universal statutory consequences like lost early release.
propositions.quote: the Crown conceded that the circumstances referred to in s. 719(3.1) need not be exceptional... The Crown argues that “circumstances” suggest facts that are particular to the offender and do not include those consequences that are universal and inherent to the statutory regime.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown concedes “circumstances” need not be exceptional but excludes universal statutory consequences like lost early release.

propositions.text: Section lacks limiting language supporting interpretation that legal regime impact is uniform for all offenders.
propositions.quote: However, the provision is devoid of any limiting language supporting this interpretation.

propositions.text: Legal regime impact varies per offender as law affects offenders differently.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the impact of the legal regime is a circumstance that is particular to each offender because the law affects offenders differently.

propositions.text: Loss of parole or early release eligibility does not affect offenders who would not have received early release anyway.
propositions.quote: For example, the loss of parole or early release eligibility will not make a difference to offenders who would not have received early release or parole in any event.

propositions.text: Legislation can change over time making its impact on offenders less uniform.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the legislation can change over time such that its impact on offenders becomes less uniform.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds section lacks limiting language; legal regime impact varies per offender; loss of parole eligibility irrelevant for some; legislation impact changes over time.

propositions.text: Section 719(3) creates a general 1:1 credit rule; 719(3.1) is an exception.
propositions.quote: The Crown submits that s. 719(3) creates a general rule of credit at a rate of 1:1, to which s. 719(3.1) is an exception.

propositions.text: If lost eligibility for early release justifies 1.5:1 credit, almost every remand offender qualifies, making exception the new general rule.
propositions.quote: If lost eligibility for early release or parole, while in pre-sentence custody, is a “circumstance” justifying enhanced credit of 1.5:1, then almost every remand offender will qualify.

propositions.text: This would render s. 719(3) irrelevant, an absurd result.
propositions.quote: This would transform the “exception” into the new “general rule” and render s. 719(3) irrelevant, an absurd result.

paragraphs.summary: Crown argues s. 719(3) is general 1:1 credit rule; s. 719(3.1) exception; broad application would make exception general and absurd.

propositions.text: Section 719(3.1) is an exception to s. 719(3), indicated by wording and marginal note.
propositions.quote: I agree that s. 719(3.1) is structured as an exception to s. 719(3) . Section 719(3.1) begins with the words “[d]espite subsection (3)” and applies only when “circumstances justify it”, which tends to indicate that it is an exception to the general rule.

propositions.text: Marginal notes, though limited in value, label s. 719(3.1) as an exception, supporting this conclusion.
propositions.quote: While marginal notes are not part of the enactment and are of limited value in statutory interpretation (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 14 ), the fact that the subsection has the marginal note “[e]xception” is consistent with this conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 719(3.1) is an exception to s. 719(3), supported by wording and marginal note.

propositions.text: Agree Crown that exception applying more often than general rule is inelegant, but argument's strength is limited for three reasons.
propositions.quote: I also agree with the Crown that it is somewhat inelegant to create an exception that applies in more cases than the general rule. However, the strength of this argument is limited for three reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees exception applying more often than general rule is inelegant but limited argument strength.

propositions.text: No general rule requires exceptions to be numerically fewer than general rules in statutory interpretation.
propositions.quote: First, there is no general rule of statutory interpretation that the circumstances falling under an exception must be numerically fewer than those falling under the general rule.

propositions.text: If criteria for departure from general proposition are met, numerical relationship is irrelevant.
propositions.quote: If the criteria that permit departure from a general proposition are satisfied, the numerical relationship is not relevant.

paragraphs.summary: Court states no rule requires exceptions to be fewer than general rules; numerical relationship irrelevant if criteria met.

propositions.text: Section 457(1) prohibits making or distributing likeness of bank-notes; s. 457(2) provides exceptions for Bank of Canada and employees.
propositions.quote: For example, s. 457(1) of the Code makes it an offence to make, publish, print, execute, issue, distribute or circulate anything in the likeness of a current bank-note. However, s. 457(2) provides exceptions, including for the Bank of Canada, its employees carrying out their duties and its contractors.

propositions.text: Most bank-notes are produced by entities covered by the exception, so exception numerically exceeds general rule.
propositions.quote: Presumably, the overwhelming majority of bank-notes are produced by the Bank of Canada, its employees, and its contractors, and therefore fall under the exception.

paragraphs.summary: Court illustrates with bank-note law where exception numerically exceeds general rule.

propositions.text: Crown accepts lack of programs and overcrowding are common and could cause exceptions under s. 719(3.1) to outnumber s. 719(3) cases.
propositions.quote: Indeed, Crown counsel accepts that the lack of programs in detention facilities and overcrowding are common problems, and could result in exceptions under s. 719(3.1) that are numerically greater than those limited by s. 719(3) .

paragraphs.summary: Crown accepts common problems could make s. 719(3.1) exceptions outnumber s. 719(3) cases.

propositions.text: Including loss of parole eligibility in 'circumstances' does not render s. 719(3) redundant due to explicit exceptions and discretion.
propositions.quote: Second, an interpretation of “circumstances” that includes loss of eligibility for parole and early release does not render subsection (3) redundant.

propositions.text: Explicit exceptions to s. 719(3.1) mean s. 719(3)'s one-for-one cap still applies in some cases.
propositions.quote: Where an accused falls under an explicit exception to s. 719(3.1) (for instance, because she has been detained for breach of bail conditions), the one-for-one cap set by s. 719(3) will apply.

propositions.text: Enhanced credit need not be granted if pre-sentence detention is due to offender's wrongful conduct; s. 719(3) remains relevant.
propositions.quote: Moreover, enhanced credit need not be granted in every case. For example, when long periods of pre-sentence detention are attributable to the wrongful conduct of the offender, enhanced credit will often be inappropriate. Section 719(3) continues to exist for such cases.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds loss of parole eligibility inclusion doesn't make s. 719(3) redundant due to exceptions and discretion.

propositions.text: Section 719(3) reflects general rationale for credit: incarceration denies liberty, so day-for-day credit is usual.
propositions.quote: Section 719(3) reflects the general rationale for giving credit. As Laskin J.A. wrote in Rezaie, at p. 721, “[i]ncarceration at any stage of the criminal process is a denial of an accused’s liberty” ― any time in jail should generally be credited day for day.

propositions.text: Section 719(3.1) reflects rationale for enhanced credit, accounting for loss of parole eligibility and harsh conditions.
propositions.quote: On the other hand, s. 719(3.1) reflects the rationale for enhanced credit. Crediting a day in pre-sentence custody as a day served is insufficient to account for the full prejudicial circumstances of remand custody; enhanced credit accounts for both loss of eligibility for parole and early release (circumstances with quantitative impact) and the harshness of the conditions (circumstances with qualitative impact).

propositions.text: Division between subsections reflects different theoretical bases for credit and enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: Thus, the division between the subsections reflects the different theoretical underpinnings of credit and enhanced credit.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 719(3) reflects general credit rationale; s. 719(3.1) reflects enhanced credit rationale including parole loss and harshness.

propositions.text: Structure builds resilience: if law changes to count pre-sentence custody for parole, s. 719(3.1) applies only to qualitative harshness.
propositions.quote: Further, this structure builds resilience into the statutory scheme. For example, if Parliament were to amend the Corrections and Conditional Release Act , so that pre-sentence custody counted for the purposes of parole eligibility and early release,[4] s. 719(3.1) would only be called upon to account for situations of qualitative harshness, and an increased number of cases would fall solely under s. 719(3) .

propositions.text: Provision structure mirrors rationales for credit and enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: The structure of the provision logically mirrors the rationales for credit and enhanced credit.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds provision structure resilient and mirrors rationales for credit and enhanced credit.

propositions.text: Parliament's intention can be determined from legislative history but with caution due to limited reliability.
propositions.quote: The intention of Parliament can be determined with reference to the legislative history, including Hansard evidence and committee debates, although the court should be mindful of the limited reliability and weight of such evidence (R. Sullivan, Sullivan on the Construction of Statutes (5th ed. 2008), at pp. 593-94 and 609).

paragraphs.summary: Court states Parliament's intention can be discerned from legislative history but cautiously due to limited reliability.

propositions.text: Parliament intended to restrict pre-sentence credit amount, capping at 1.5 days per day in detention.
propositions.quote: Parliament clearly intended to restrict the amount of pre-sentence credit. This is plain from the cap of 1.5 days credit for every day spent in detention.

propositions.text: Justice Minister stated overly generous credit harms justice administration and public perception; two-for-one credit must be curtailed.
propositions.quote: It is also consistent with statements made by the then-Justice Minister, before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Justice and Human Rights, on May 6, 2009: The practice of awarding overly generous credit can put the administration of justice into disrepute because it creates the impression that offenders are getting more lenient sentences than they deserve. The public does not understand how the final sentence reflects the seriousness of the crime. For these reasons, the current practice of routinely awarding two-for-one credit must be curtailed.

propositions.text: This objective is achieved regardless of what circumstances justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1).
propositions.quote: This objective is achieved regardless of what circumstances may justify the use of enhanced credit in s. 719(3.1) .

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Parliament intended to restrict credit to 1.5:1; Minister's statement supports this; objective achieved regardless of enhanced credit circumstances.

propositions.text: Parliament intended credit granting process to be transparent and understandable via ss. 719(3.2) and 719(3.3) requiring reasons and credit stated.
propositions.quote: Parliament also intended that the process of granting credit under s. 719 should be more transparent and easily understood by the public. It achieved this end through the insertion of ss. 719(3.2) and 719(3.3), which provide that judges should give reasons for granting credit and state both the fit sentence and the amount of credit granted.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Parliament intended transparency in credit granting via ss. 719(3.2) and 719(3.3).

propositions.text: Intention of Parliament on what 'circumstances' justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) is unclear and contradictory.
propositions.quote: However, I agree with Beveridge J.A. and Cronk J.A. that the intention of Parliament with respect to what “circumstances” may justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) is far less clear and even contradictory (Carvery, at paras. 79-82; Summers, at paras. 82-88).

propositions.text: Legislative history does not assist in answering what circumstances justify enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the legislative history is of no assistance in answering this question.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Parliament's intention on 'circumstances' for enhanced credit unclear; legislative history unhelpful.

propositions.text: Parliament presumed to know legal context; prior practice of awarding enhanced credit for quantitative and qualitative consequences was entrenched and endorsed by this Court.
propositions.quote: Parliament is presumed to know the legal context in which it legislates.[5] The practice of using the former s. 719(3) to award enhanced credit for both the quantitative and qualitative consequences of pre-sentence detention was deeply entrenched in our sentencing system. This practice was expressly endorsed by this Court in Wust, where the Court identified the loss of eligibility for early release and parole as a reason justifying enhanced credit.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Parliament presumed to know legal context; prior enhanced credit practice was entrenched and endorsed by Court.

propositions.text: Parliament can exclude these circumstances but unlikely intended to overturn long-standing practice without explicit language.
propositions.quote: Parliament does, of course, have the power to exclude these circumstances from consideration (barring a constitutional challenge). However, it strikes me as inconceivable that Parliament intended to overturn a principled and long-standing sentencing practice, without using explicit language, by instead relying on inferences that could possibly be drawn from the order of certain provisions in the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Parliament unlikely intended to overturn long-standing practice without explicit language.

propositions.text: Parliament explicitly imposed 1.5:1 credit cap, a clear departure from prior practice, with no indication of altering reasons for enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: Rather, it seems more likely that Parliament intended to do what it did explicitly. The amendments clearly impose a cap on the rate at which credit can be awarded, at 1.5:1. This is a substantial and clear departure from pre-TISA practice. Having made its intention so clear on that point, Parliament gave no indication it intended to alter the reasons for which enhanced credit can be granted.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Parliament explicitly capped credit at 1.5:1 but gave no indication of altering enhanced credit reasons.

propositions.text: Neither provision language nor external evidence shows clear intention to abolish principled rationale for enhanced credit.
propositions.quote: In my view, neither the language of the provision nor the external evidence demonstrates a clear intention to abolish one of the principled rationales for enhanced credit.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes no clear intention to abolish principled rationale for enhanced credit.

propositions.text: Sections 719(3) and 719(3.1) are part of overall sentencing scheme and should be interpreted consistently with sentencing principles in Part XXIII.
propositions.quote: While the foregoing is sufficient to dispose of the appeal, I recognize that ss. 719(3) and 719(3.1) do not exist in isolation, but form part of the overall sentencing scheme in the Criminal Code . As the legislature is presumed to have created a coherent, consistent and harmonious statutory scheme, s. 719 should be interpreted in a manner that is consistent with the principles and purposes of sentencing set out in Part XXIII of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: Sentencing principles include denouncing unlawful conduct, deterrence, separation, rehabilitation, reparations, and promoting offender responsibility.
propositions.quote: Sections 718, 718.1 and 718.2 of the Code provide: 718. The fundamental purpose of sentencing is to contribute, along with crime prevention initiatives, to respect for the law and the maintenance of a just, peaceful and safe society by imposing just sanctions that have one or more of the following objectives: (a) to denounce unlawful conduct; (b) to deter the offender and other persons from committing offences; (c) to separate offenders from society, where necessary; (d) to assist in rehabilitating offenders; (e) to provide reparations for harm done to victims or to the community; and (f) to promote a sense of responsibility in offenders, and acknowledgment of the harm done to victims and to the community. 718.1 A sentence must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender. 718.2 A court that imposes a sentence shall also take into consideration the following principles: . . . (b) a sentence should be similar to sentences imposed on similar offenders for similar offences committed in similar circumstances;

paragraphs.summary: Court finds ss. 719(3) and (3.1) part of sentencing scheme; sentencing principles include denouncing, deterrence, rehabilitation, reparations, and proportionality.

propositions.text: Interpretation excluding loss of parole eligibility means unbail offenders serve longer sentences than similar bail-granted offenders.
propositions.quote: As Beveridge J.A. and Cronk J.A. recognized, an interpretation of s. 719(3.1) that does not account for loss of eligibility for early release and parole during remand custody means that offenders who do not receive bail will serve longer sentences than otherwise identical offenders who are granted bail.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-makers found excluding parole loss means unbail offenders serve longer sentences than similar bail-granted offenders.

propositions.text: A rule causing longer sentences for offenders without bail violates the parity principle in s. 718.2(b).
propositions.quote: A rule that results in longer sentences for offenders who do not obtain bail, compared to otherwise identical offenders, does not result in “similar . . . sentences imposed on similar offenders for similar offences committed in similar circumstances”: s. 718.2(b).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that sentencing rules causing longer sentences for offenders without bail violate the parity principle in s. 718.2(b).

propositions.text: Parity does not require absolute equality and enhanced credit is ineffective to achieve equality between offenders.
propositions.quote: The Crown says that parity does not require absolute equality and that in any event, enhanced credit is an ineffective tool to achieve equality between offenders, since it is premised on both being released on their statutory release date (after two thirds of their sentence).

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues parity does not require absolute equality and enhanced credit is ineffective to achieve equality between offenders.

propositions.text: Structural sentencing differences based on irrelevant criteria violate the parity principle.
propositions.quote: Nonetheless, a rule that creates structural differences in sentences, based on criteria irrelevant to sentencing, is inconsistent with the principle of parity.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that structural sentencing differences based on irrelevant criteria violate the parity principle.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal wrongly relied on proportionality; proportionality concerns just sanctions, not comparisons with similar offenders.
propositions.quote: The Crown also says that the Court of Appeal’s reliance on the sentencing principle of proportionality was misplaced. Proportionality is simply concerned with the imposition of a just sanction in a particular case; any comparison with similar offenders is irrelevant.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues the Court of Appeal wrongly relied on proportionality, which concerns just sanctions, not comparisons with similar offenders.

propositions.text: Sentences cannot be proportionate if incarceration length depends on bail eligibility, which is unrelated to offence gravity or offender responsibility.
propositions.quote: However, it is difficult to see how sentences can reliably be “proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender” (s. 718.1) when the length of incarceration is also a product of the offender’s ability to obtain bail, which is frequently dependent on totally different criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds sentences cannot be proportionate if incarceration length depends on bail eligibility unrelated to offence gravity or offender responsibility.

propositions.text: Judicial interim release depends on assurances often unavailable to vulnerable offenders lacking support or financial means.
propositions.quote: Judicial interim release requires the judge to be confident that, amongst other things, the accused will neither flee nor reoffend while on bail. When an accused is able to deposit money, or be released to family and friends acting as sureties (who often pledge money themselves), this can help provide the court with such assurance. Unfortunately, those without either a support network of family and friends or financial means cannot provide these assurances.

propositions.text: The John Howard Society submitted that vulnerable and impoverished offenders are less able to access bail.
propositions.quote: Consequently, as the intervener the John Howard Society submitted, this means that vulnerable and impoverished offenders are less able to access bail.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds judicial interim release depends on assurances often unavailable to vulnerable offenders; the John Howard Society submits such offenders have less access to bail.

propositions.text: Aboriginal people are more likely denied bail and overrepresented in remand custody.
propositions.quote: For example, Aboriginal people are more likely to be denied bail, and make up a disproportionate share of the population in remand custody.[6]

propositions.text: Sentencing harsher for vulnerable offenders due to isolation and inability to pay violates parity and proportionality principles.
propositions.quote: A system that results in consistently longer, harsher sentences for vulnerable members of society, not based on the wrongfulness of their conduct but because of their isolation and inability to pay, can hardly be said to be assigning sentences in line with the principles of parity and proportionality.

propositions.text: Accounting for loss of early release eligibility through enhanced credit addresses this concern.
propositions.quote: Accounting for loss of early release eligibility through enhanced credit responds to this concern.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Aboriginal people are disproportionately denied bail; harsher sentences for vulnerable offenders violate parity and proportionality; enhanced credit addresses this.

propositions.text: Loss of eligibility for early release and parole may justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1).
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I conclude that the “circumstances” justifying enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) may include loss of eligibility for early release and parole.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes loss of eligibility for early release and parole may justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1).

propositions.text: Reading limiting language into s. 719(3.1) to exclude loss of early release eligibility is unsupported and inconsistent with Code principles and prior practice.
propositions.quote: To conclude otherwise, it would be necessary for the Court to read limiting language into s. 719(3.1) that is simply not there. Such an interpretation would result in sentences inconsistent with the Code’s own statement of principles, and would presume that the legislature intended to abolish the quantitative rationale for enhanced credit — that offenders should not be punished more severely because they were not released on bail — without clear language. And this despite the well-established practice, endorsed by this Court in Wust in the year 2000, that enhanced credit can be justified based upon the loss of eligibility for parole and early release. Such a conclusion is not plausible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds excluding loss of early release eligibility from s. 719(3.1) is unsupported and inconsistent with Code principles and prior practice.

propositions.text: Judges may credit at most 1.5 days per day served for pre-sentence custody when circumstances warrant, following Wust's analytical approach.
propositions.quote: In determining credit for pre-sentence custody, judges may credit at most 1.5 days for every day served where circumstances warrant. While there is now a statutory maximum, the analytical approach endorsed in Wust otherwise remains unchanged.

propositions.text: Credit should consider quantitative rationale (lost early release eligibility) and qualitative rationale (harsh detention conditions).
propositions.quote: Judges should continue to assign credit on the basis of the quantitative rationale, to account for lost eligibility for early release and parole during pre-sentence custody, and the qualitative rationale, to account for the relative harshness of the conditions in detention centres.

paragraphs.summary: The court states judges may credit up to 1.5 days per day served for pre-sentence custody, considering lost early release eligibility and harsh detention conditions.

propositions.text: Loss of early release alone generally justifies 1.5:1 credit; lower rates apply if detention due to offender's bad conduct or parole unlikely.
propositions.quote: The loss of early release, taken alone, will generally be a sufficient basis to award credit at the rate of 1.5 to 1, even if the conditions of detention are not particularly harsh, and parole is unlikely. Of course, a lower rate may be appropriate when detention was a result of the offender’s bad conduct, or the offender is likely to obtain neither early release nor parole.

propositions.text: Statutory exceptions in s. 719(3.1) limit credit to 1:1; credit applies only if pre-sentence detention results from the offence being sentenced.
propositions.quote: When the statutory exceptions within s. 719(3.1) are engaged, credit may only be given at a rate of 1 to 1. Moreover, s. 719 is engaged only where the pre-sentence detention is a result of the offence for which the offender is being sentenced.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains loss of early release usually justifies 1.5:1 credit; exceptions limit credit to 1:1; credit applies only if detention results from the offence.

propositions.text: Capping pre-sentence credit at 1.5:1 means it may not fully compensate harsh detention but should not restrict warranted credit.
propositions.quote: The unavoidable consequence of capping pre-sentence credit at this rate is that it is insufficient to compensate for the harshness of pre-sentence detention in all cases. However, this does not mean that credit should be scaled back in order to “leave room at the top” of the scale for the most egregious cases. A cap is a cut-off and means simply that the upper limit will be reached in more cases. It should not lead judges to deny or restrict credit when it is warranted.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the 1.5:1 credit cap may not fully compensate harsh detention but should not restrict warranted credit.

propositions.text: Offenders suffering harsh treatment in detention can seek remedies under s. 24(1) of the Charter.
propositions.quote: Indeed, individuals who have suffered particularly harsh treatment, such as assaults in detention, can often look to other remedies, including under s. 24(1) of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds offenders suffering harsh treatment in detention can seek remedies under s. 24(1) of the Charter.

propositions.text: Sentencing judges must give reasons and state details for any credit granted under ss. 719(3.2) and 719(3.3).
propositions.quote: The sentencing judge is also required to give reasons for any credit granted (s. 719(3.2)) and to state “the amount of time spent in custody, the term of imprisonment that would have been imposed before any credit was granted, the amount of time credited, if any, and the sentence imposed” (s. 719(3.3)).

propositions.text: This requirement is not onerous but important for public understanding of sentencing and credit reasons.
propositions.quote: This is not a particularly onerous requirement, but plays an important role in explaining the nature of the sentencing process, and the reasons for giving credit, to the public.

paragraphs.summary: The court states judges must give reasons and details for credit granted, an important but not onerous requirement for public understanding.

propositions.text: Loss of remission or parole does not automatically require credit above 1:1 (Carvery, para. 60).
propositions.quote: For many offenders, the loss of eligibility for early release and parole will justify credit at a rate of 1.5:1. However, as Beveridge J.A. concluded, it is not an “automatic or a foregone conclusion that a judge must grant credit at more than 1:1 based on loss of remission or parole” (Carvery, at para. 60).

paragraphs.summary: The Court reports Beveridge J.A. found loss of remission or parole does not automatically require credit above 1:1.

propositions.text: It is not onerous for offenders to establish entitlement to credit above 1:1 due to lost remission or parole (Carvery, para. 66).
propositions.quote: As Beveridge J.A. wrote: . . . it would not be onerous for most offenders to establish that they would have earned remission or been granted parole, and hence, it is not likely to be a rare occurrence for an offender to be worthy of a credit of more than 1:1. [para. 66]

paragraphs.summary: The Court reports Beveridge J.A. found offenders can usually establish entitlement to credit above 1:1 due to lost remission or parole.

propositions.text: Sentencing courts should not inquire into likelihood of parole as it relates to sentence administration, not sentencing.
propositions.quote: The Crown says it is not appropriate for the sentencing court to inquire into the likelihood that a particular offender will receive parole because considerations relating to the administration of the sentence are irrelevant to sentencing.

propositions.text: Reducing sentence by speculation about release timing is improper.
propositions.quote: Further, it is improper to reduce a sentence by granting enhanced credit based on speculation about when the offender may be released.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues sentencing courts should not inquire into parole likelihood or reduce sentences based on speculative release timing.

propositions.text: Judges can assess offender's future conduct and likelihood of parole similar to rehabilitation prospects.
propositions.quote: However, judges are often called upon to make assessments about an offender’s future, for example by considering prospects for rehabilitation. I see no reason why judges cannot draw similar inferences with respect to the offender’s future conduct in prison and the likelihood of parole or early release.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds judges can assess offender's future conduct and parole likelihood similar to rehabilitation prospects.

propositions.text: Offender must prove entitlement to enhanced credit; pre-sentence detention usually infers lost early release eligibility.
propositions.quote: The onus is on the offender to demonstrate that he should be awarded enhanced credit as a result of his pre-sentence detention. Generally speaking, the fact that pre-sentence detention has occurred will usually be sufficient to give rise to an inference that the offender has lost eligibility for parole or early release, justifying enhanced credit.

propositions.text: Crown may rebut inference; dangerous offenders or poor conduct may justify withholding enhanced credit; extensive evidence rarely needed.
propositions.quote: Of course, the Crown may respond by challenging such an inference. There will be particularly dangerous offenders who have committed certain serious offences for whom early release and parole are simply not available.[7] Similarly, if the accused’s conduct in jail suggests that he is unlikely to be granted early release or parole, the judge may be justified in withholding enhanced credit. Extensive evidence will rarely be necessary.

propositions.text: A practical, non-elaborate approach is required to avoid complicating sentencing.
propositions.quote: A practical approach is required that does not complicate or prolong the sentencing process.

paragraphs.summary: The court rules offender must prove enhanced credit entitlement; Crown may rebut; practical approach avoids complicating sentencing.

propositions.text: Offender bears onus for qualitative rationale; extensive evidence usually unnecessary; conditions often agreed or well known.
propositions.quote: As well, when evaluating the qualitative rationale for granting enhanced credit, the onus is on the offender, but it will generally not be necessary to lead extensive evidence. Judges have dealt with claims for enhanced credit for many years. The conditions and overcrowding in remand centres are generally well known and often subject to agreement between the parties; there is no reason this helpful practice should not continue.

propositions.text: TISA capped enhanced credit but did not change process for determining credit amount.
propositions.quote: There is no need for a new and elaborate process — the TISA introduced a cap on the amount of enhanced credit that may be awarded, but did not alter the process for determining the amount of credit to apply.

paragraphs.summary: The court states offender bears onus for qualitative rationale; extensive evidence usually unnecessary; TISA capped credit but did not change process.

propositions.text: Quebec Director argues personal circumstances unrelated to detention conditions cannot justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1)
propositions.quote: The intervener the Quebec Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions argues that factors based on the personal circumstances of a particular inmate, with no relation to the conditions in which he or she was detained, cannot justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) .

paragraphs.summary: The Quebec Director argues personal circumstances unrelated to detention conditions cannot justify enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1).

propositions.text: Credit for pre-sentence detention ensures equal punishment whether released on bail or remanded in custody pre-trial
propositions.quote: It has long been recognized that credit for pre-sentence detention is intended to ensure that individuals are punished equally, whether they are released on bail or remanded in custody prior to trial.

propositions.text: Circumstances relevant to relative harshness of pre-sentence custody versus serving sentence are relevant
propositions.quote: Consequently, any circumstances that speak to the relative harshness of pre-sentence custody, as opposed to serving a sentence, are relevant.

paragraphs.summary: The court states credit for pre-sentence detention ensures equal punishment and relevant circumstances relate to relative harshness of custody versus sentence.

propositions.text: Factors like reduced moral culpability or first conviction are not relevant to relative harshness of pre-trial detention
propositions.quote: On this basis, it is difficult to see how factors such as reduced moral culpability of the offender, or the fact that it was a first conviction, could be relevant circumstances with respect to the relative harshness of pre-trial detention.

propositions.text: Early guilty plea, acceptance of responsibility, and remorse relate to sentencing, not credit under s. 719(3) or s. 719(3.1)
propositions.quote: The fact that the respondent entered an early guilty plea, accepted responsibility for his actions, and expressed sincere remorse are generally only relevant to the determination of a fit sentence and not to assigning credit under s. 719(3) or s. 719(3.1) .

propositions.text: Considering sentencing factors again for credit is 'double dipping'
propositions.quote: To consider them again is what was described as “double dipping”.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds factors like moral culpability and remorse relate to sentencing, not credit, and considering them again is 'double dipping'.

propositions.text: Sentencing judge did not err in granting enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) based on loss of early release and parole eligibility
propositions.quote: The sentencing judge did not err in law by granting enhanced credit under s. 719(3.1) on the basis of the respondent’s loss of eligibility for early release and parole.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the sentencing judge did not err in granting enhanced credit based on loss of early release and parole eligibility.

propositions.text: Sentencing judge focused on lack of parole access, not guilty plea or remorse, when assessing credit
propositions.quote: The sentencing judge in this case did not rely on improper factors in assessing credit for pre-trial detention. In his analysis of the appropriate credit, the judge focused on the lack of access to parole, not the respondent’s guilty plea and remorse (paras. 39-43).

propositions.text: Discussion of guilty plea and remorse was directed at sentencing generally, not credit
propositions.quote: His discussion of the latter factors was directed at sentencing generally.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the sentencing judge focused on parole access, not guilty plea or remorse, for credit; those factors related to sentencing generally.

propositions.text: Cronk J.A. suggested guilty plea and remorse relevant only to likelihood of parole, not independent credit factors
propositions.quote: To the extent Cronk J.A. referred to these considerations, at para. 124 of her decision, I take her to be suggesting they are relevant for the limited purpose of determining whether the respondent was likely to be granted parole (which is relevant to whether the respondent, in fact, lost the opportunity for parole and early release). She did not treat them as independent circumstances justifying enhanced credit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Cronk J.A. saw guilty plea and remorse as relevant only to parole likelihood, not independent credit factors.

propositions.text: Cronk J.A. agreed no basis to think respondent would be denied parole or early release
propositions.quote: I agree with Cronk J.A. that there was no basis to think that the respondent would be denied parole or early release.

propositions.text: Cronk J.A. noted Crown counsel conceded respondent's good behaviour in remand custody and no negative effect on release eligibility
propositions.quote: She said of Crown counsel at trial: By her reference to the likelihood of early parole for the respondent, she also conceded, in effect, the respondent’s good behaviour while in remand custody. Certainly, she did not suggest that the respondent’s conduct would in any way disentitle him to earned remission or negatively affect his statutory release and parole eligibility. [para. 125]

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Cronk J.A. that no basis existed to deny parole; Crown counsel conceded good behaviour and no negative effect on release eligibility.

propositions.text: Little evidence on parole likelihood but no serious challenge to conclusion respondent likely accessed parole and early release
propositions.quote: While little evidence was available on this point, there is no serious challenge to the conclusion that the respondent was likely to access parole and early release.

propositions.text: Appropriate to grant credit at 1.5 days per day in detention based on quantitative rationale for enhanced credit
propositions.quote: Therefore, it was appropriate to grant credit at a rate of 1.5 days for every day in detention on the basis of the quantitative rationale for enhanced credit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious challenge to parole likelihood and approves credit at 1.5 days per day detained based on quantitative rationale.

propositions.text: Dismiss the appeal
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal. Appeal dismissed.

propositions.text: Lists solicitors for appellant, respondent, and interveners
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the appellant: Attorney General of Ontario, Toronto. Solicitors for the respondent: Brennan Smart Law Office, Kitchener; Russell Silverstein & Associate, Toronto. Solicitor for the intervener the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions of Quebec: Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions of Quebec, Montréal. Solicitors for the intervener the British Columbia Civil Liberties Association: Bull, Housser & Tupper, Vancouver. Solicitors for the intervener the Criminal Lawyers’ Association of Ontario: Russell Silverstein & Associate, Toronto. Solicitors for the intervener the John Howard Society of Canada: Polley Faith, Toronto. Solicitors for the intervener the Canadian Civil Liberties Association: Lerners, Toronto.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and lists solicitors for all parties and interveners.
